title: Vectors in a right-handed coordinate system
objective: Resolve and combine three-dimensional vectors and distinguish projections, dot products, and cross products with their directions and units.
why: A force, velocity, or displacement has a direction as well as a size. Adding its numerical size to another size can give the wrong mechanical prediction. Components let you keep direction through a calculation, while vector products distinguish quantities such as work and torque. These tools will support every later motion and force model.

sections.heading: Choose axes before assigning signs
paragraphs: A scalar is specified by one value in a unit, without a spatial direction. Mass, elapsed time, and energy are scalars. A vector has magnitude and direction: position, displacement, velocity, and force are examples. A scalar can be signed, so a negative value alone does not make something a vector.

Choose mutually perpendicular x, y, and z axes and state their positive directions. We use a right-handed system: the positive z direction follows the right-hand rule from +x toward +y. For an xy drawing with +x to the right and +y upward, +z points toward you, out of the page. Keeping this convention fixed is essential when computing a cross product.

Write $\mathbf A=A_x\hat{\mathbf i}+A_y\hat{\mathbf j}+A_z\hat{\mathbf k}$, or list the components as $(A_x,A_y,A_z)$. The symbols with hats are dimensionless unit vectors along the chosen axes. The components carry the vector's physical units. A negative component means an opposite contribution along that axis; it does not mean the vector has a negative length.

Components depend on your coordinates, but physical predictions must remain consistent when you transform every quantity to a new coordinate system. Changing only one vector's axes while leaving another in the old axes makes a dot or cross product meaningless. The practice here always uses one shared orthonormal frame.

sections.heading: Position, displacement, and path length
paragraphs: A position vector points from a chosen origin to a location. Displacement between two events is final position minus initial position: $\Delta\mathbf r=\mathbf r_f-\mathbf r_i$. Subtract corresponding components in the same order. The displacement points from the initial location to the final location.

A fixed change of origin adds the same offset to both positions, so it cancels from their difference. This is why displacement does not depend on where you place a fixed origin, although each position does. Later, motion relative to moving observers requires a separate velocity transformation.

The magnitude of displacement is the straight-line separation of the endpoints. Distance traveled follows the path and cannot be smaller than that separation. If you move 3 m east and then 3 m west, displacement is zero while distance is 6 m. A closed path can have substantial traveled length with no net displacement.

The zero vector has every component equal to zero. It has magnitude zero and no unique direction. Assigning it a direction along +x is an extra convention that has no physical justification. Division by its magnitude cannot create a unit vector.

sections.heading: Combine components, then find a magnitude
paragraphs: Vector addition combines corresponding components: $\mathbf A+\mathbf B=(A_x+B_x,A_y+B_y,A_z+B_z)$. Geometrically, placing B's tail at A's head leads to the same resultant as this component calculation. Addition is commutative; exchanging A and B does not change the sum.

For orthonormal Cartesian axes, the magnitude is $|\mathbf A|=\sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2+A_z^2}$. This is the three-dimensional Pythagorean relation. Squaring removes component signs, and the final square root selects a nonnegative length. The signs must still be retained in the components themselves.

In general $|\mathbf A+\mathbf B|$ is not $|\mathbf A|+|\mathbf B|$. The sum of magnitudes gives an upper bound on the resultant magnitude, with equality when nonzero vectors point in the same direction. Opposite vectors can cancel. This supplies a useful plausibility check after calculation.

Multiplication by a scalar c scales every component. The magnitude becomes $|c|\,|\mathbf A|$. If c is negative, the direction reverses as well as scaling. A dimensionless scalar changes magnitude without changing units; multiplication by a time or mass changes the physical units and therefore the kind of quantity being modeled.

sections.heading: Describe a direction without losing its quadrant
paragraphs: For a nonzero vector, $\hat{\mathbf A}=\mathbf A/|\mathbf A|$ is a unit vector in the same direction. Its components are dimensionless and their squares sum to one. Dividing each component by its own absolute value would produce sign indicators, not generally a unit vector.

In a plane, a magnitude A and angle theta measured counterclockwise from +x give $A_x=A\cos\theta$ and $A_y=A\sin\theta$. The component units remain those of A. A three-dimensional vector generally needs two angles or a complete set of direction components; a single xy direction does not locate it in space.

When recovering an angle, first inspect both component signs. The ordinary arctangent of $A_y/A_x$ cannot by itself distinguish opposite quadrants and is unavailable as a direct quotient when $A_x=0$. A quadrant-aware atan2 function uses both arguments. Here planar direction questions request degrees in $[0,360)$; convert the calculator's result to that convention.

For example, (-3,4) lies in quadrant II. Its length is 5, and its direction is about 126.87 degrees, not -53.13 degrees. Check by computing $5\cos\theta$ and $5\sin\theta$: the first must be negative and the second positive. A calculator mode mismatch changes the values even if the component formulas were selected correctly.

sections.heading: The dot product measures alignment
paragraphs: The scalar or dot product is $\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B=A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$. Multiply matching components and add the signed products. For nonzero inputs, it also equals $|\mathbf A||\mathbf B|\cos\theta$, where theta is the angle between them. The result is one scalar, not three components.

A positive dot product indicates a positive projection along the other vector, a negative value indicates an opposing projection, and zero indicates perpendicular nonzero vectors or at least one zero input. A dot product with itself equals squared magnitude, so $\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf A\ge0$. The two-vector dot product need not be positive.

The signed scalar projection of A onto the direction of a nonzero B is $\mathbf A\cdot\hat{\mathbf B}=(\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B)/|\mathbf B|$. Its units are those of A. Its absolute value cannot exceed A's magnitude. A vector projection instead multiplies that scalar by the unit direction of B, producing a vector along the selected line.

For a constant force acting through a displacement, work is $W=\mathbf F\cdot\Delta\mathbf r$. Its units are N m, named joules. Force perpendicular to displacement does no work in this model even though the force need not be zero. The later work lesson extends the product to a path integral for a varying force.

sections.heading: The cross product records an oriented perpendicular direction
paragraphs: The vector or cross product has components $\mathbf A\times\mathbf B=(A_yB_z-A_zB_y,\ A_zB_x-A_xB_z,\ A_xB_y-A_yB_x)$. Notice the cyclic order x, y, z. An easy error is to reverse only the middle component's subtraction. Write the full component rule or expand a determinant with its alternating signs.

Its magnitude is $|\mathbf A||\mathbf B|\sin\theta$ for the angle between nonzero vectors, and its direction follows the right-hand rule from A toward B. In our axes, $\hat{\mathbf i}\times\hat{\mathbf j}=\hat{\mathbf k}$. Parallel vectors, opposite vectors, or a zero input produce a zero cross product.

Order matters: $\mathbf B\times\mathbf A=-\mathbf A\times\mathbf B$. This antisymmetry differs from the commutative dot product. Two nonzero cross products from exchanged inputs have the same magnitude and opposite direction. The zero result equals its own negative, but still has no unique direction.

For torque about a chosen origin, $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$, where r points from the origin to the point where the force acts. Use that order. Torque is expressed as N m and remains a vector, unlike scalar work in joules. Matching base dimensions do not make work and torque interchangeable.

Check a computed cross product by taking its dot product with each input; both must vanish. Also check its magnitude using the angle or the identity $|\mathbf A\times\mathbf B|^2+(\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B)^2=|\mathbf A|^2|\mathbf B|^2$. Perpendicularity alone is insufficient: it would also accept the opposite vector or a scaled perpendicular vector.

sections.heading: Use a drawing as evidence, not as hidden data
paragraphs: A two-dimensional drawing of a three-dimensional vector omits information. The projection of (0,0,5) onto the xy plane is a point, but the full vector has magnitude 5. A picture cannot replace the labeled z component. The investigation therefore provides a full component table beside its planar projection.

Before using any vector result in mechanics, name the inputs and their units, verify that they share the same coordinate frame, state the operation, and interpret the result. Vector addition applies to quantities of the same physical type. Dot and cross products multiply units, but their physical meaning depends on which quantities were supplied.

Retain exact square roots when a magnitude or normalized component is requested exactly. Equivalent forms such as $1/\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt2/2$ represent the same value. Round only the explicitly approximate angle questions. The checks in this lesson accept equivalent exact fractions and radicals rather than relying on one printed expression.

examples.title: Recover a three-dimensional displacement
examples.prompt: A sensor begins at (1,-2,3) m and ends at (-3,4,0) m. Find displacement, its magnitude, and a unit direction.

steps.reason: Subtract the initial position from the final position on each axis.
Square and sum all three components before taking the nonnegative root.
Divide by the single nonzero magnitude. The length unit cancels.
The displacement reconstructs the final position and the unit direction has length one.

examples.conclusion: Displacement is (-4,6,-3) m. Its magnitude is sqrt(61) m; a traveled path between the same endpoints could be longer.

examples.title: Choose the correct planar quadrant
examples.prompt: A planar displacement has x=-3 m and y=4 m. Find its length and counterclockwise direction from +x in [0,360) degrees.

steps.reason: Magnitude is nonnegative even though the x component is negative.
The component signs place the vector in quadrant II. The acute reference angle must be measured from the negative x direction.
Reconstructing the components checks both the magnitude and the quadrant.

examples.conclusion: The length is 5 m and the direction is 126.87 degrees to the nearest 0.01 degree. Using only arctan(4/-3) without a quadrant adjustment would point the wrong way.

examples.title: Separate a dot product from a scalar projection
examples.prompt: Let A=(3,4,0) m and let the dimensionless direction vector B=(-2,1,2). Calculate A dot B and the scalar projection of A onto B.

steps.reason: Multiply corresponding components and add; a negative result is permitted.
The direction vector has not yet been normalized.
Divide the dot product by B's magnitude to obtain projection onto a unit direction.
A projection cannot have a greater absolute length than its original vector.

examples.conclusion: The dot product is -2 m and the signed scalar projection is -2/3 m. B was dimensionless; if B were a force in newtons, the dot product would instead have work units.

examples.title: Compute and independently check a torque direction
examples.prompt: A force F=(3,0,4) N acts at r=(1,2,-1) m relative to a pivot. Calculate r cross F.

steps.reason: The x component combines the y and z components in their stated order.
Cycle the axes. Preserve the subtraction order for the middle component.
The torque must be perpendicular to the position vector.
The torque must also be perpendicular to the force.
The product-magnitude identity checks its length using |r|²=6, |F|²=25, and r dot F=-1.

examples.conclusion: The torque is (8,-7,-6) N m. F cross r would have all three signs reversed. The selected pivot is part of this result's definition.

examples.title: Interpret a zero resultant without erasing the path
examples.prompt: Two successive displacements are (2,-1,3) m and (-2,1,-3) m. Compare net displacement with total length of the two straight segments.

steps.reason: Path lengths are nonnegative scalars, so the two segment lengths add even though the vectors cancel.
A zero denominator prevents normalization; no unique direction is selected by a return to the starting point.

examples.conclusion: The object returned to its initial position after traveling 2sqrt(14) m. Zero displacement does not imply no motion.

guided.title: Finish the vector products
guided.setup: In right-handed axes, dimensionless A=(2,-1,0) and B=(0,3,4). Compute A dot B and A cross B.
before: The dot product is the sum 2(0)+(-1)(3)+0(4).
The x component of A cross B is (-1)(4)-0(3).
For the y component use Az Bx - Ax Bz; for z use Ax By - Ay Bx.

question.prompt: Enter the scalar product and all three cross-product components. Then predict what exchanging A and B would do.

fields.label: Effect of exchanging A and B

options.label: Both products reverse sign
options.feedback: The dot product is commutative, so it stays -3. Only the cross product reverses sign.

options.label: The dot product stays the same; the cross product reverses sign
options.feedback: Component multiplication makes the dot product commutative; the cross product's oriented differences are antisymmetric.

options.label: Neither product changes
options.feedback: Exchanging the cross-product operands reverses its right-hand-rule direction.

hints: The dot product is -3. For the cross product, keep A first in every component expression.
The cross-product x component is -4 and its y component is -8.
The cross-product z component is 6. Check (-4,-8,6) dot (2,-1,0)=0 and dot (0,3,4)=0.
explanation: A dot B=-3 and A cross B=(-4,-8,6).
The scalar product is unchanged by swapping. B cross A=(4,8,-6). Both perpendicularity checks vanish.
question.answerSummary: Dot -3; cross (-4,-8,6); swapping changes only the cross-product sign.

guided.after: A perpendicularity check catches many component errors, but a sign-reversed vector is also perpendicular. Check the operand order and right-handed convention as well.

interaction.prompt: Predict the dot and cross products of A and B. Check the result, swap the inputs, and explain what stays unchanged. Then compare parallel, opposite, and zero vectors, including one that has only a z component.

summary: State a shared coordinate frame and retain signed components. Magnitudes are nonnegative.
Displacement is final position minus initial position; distance traveled follows the path.
Normalize with one common nonzero magnitude. A zero vector has no unique direction.
A dot product is a signed scalar; a scalar projection divides by the magnitude of the direction vector.
A cross product is a vector with a right-hand-rule direction. Exchanging its inputs reverses the sign.
Check vector results using reconstruction, units, perpendicularity, magnitude identities, and simple limiting cases. A planar projection is not the full 3D vector.
retrieval: For A=(1,2,0) and B=(0,-1,3), find their sum, dot product, and cross product. Predict the products after swapping them. Explain why a vector with only a z component can disappear in an xy drawing without being the zero vector.
